responses.text:
def merge_intervals(intervals):
    """Merge overlapping closed intervals.

    Args:
        intervals: A list of [start, end] pairs (or tuples) representing
            closed intervals, where start <= end.

    Returns:
        A new list of merged intervals, sorted by start value, with no
        overlapping or touching intervals.

    Time Complexity:
        O(n log n) due to sorting the input intervals, where n is the
        number of intervals. The subsequent merge pass is O(n).
    """
    if not intervals:
        return []

    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[0])
    merged = [list(sorted_intervals[0])]

    for start, end in sorted_intervals[1:]:
        last = merged[-1]
        if start <= last[1]:
            last[1] = max(last[1], end)
        else:
            merged.append([start, end])

    return merged


assert merge_intervals([[1, 3"], [2, 6"], [8, 10"], [15, 18"]]) == [[1, 6"], [8, 10"], [15, 18"]]
assert merge_intervals([[1, 4"], [4, 5"]]) == [[1, 5"]]
assert merge_intervals([]) == []

Round2 paired single-stream workload; ignore this marker.
Explain why database indexes speed up reads but slow down writes. Use a concrete library-catalog analogy, discuss selectivity and give one practical rule for choosing a compound index. Write about 220 words.
responses.text:
An index is like a library’s card catalog: instead of scanning every shelf (a table scan), you look up a subject heading and jump straight to the right books. Reads speed up because the index is sorted and compact, letting the database binary-search or range-scan rather than examine every row.

Writes slow down because every insert, update, or delete must also maintain the catalog: add a card, refile cards when pages shift, and keep the index consistent with the shelves. More indexes mean more bookkeeping per write.

Selectivity measures how discriminating an index is. A catalog of unique ISBNs is highly selective—each entry points to one book—so lookups are fast. A subject heading like “fiction” is low-selectivity: thousands of books share it, so the index narrows the search only a little, and the database may still read many rows.

Practical rule for compound indexes: order columns by equality first,range second. For queries like WHERE author = 'Orwell' AND year BETWEEN 1930 AND 1950, build (author, year). The leading column filters to a small set, and the second column efficiently handles the range within that set. Reversing the order (year, author) forces scanning many years before applying the author filter, reducing the benefit.

responses.prompt:
Round2 paired single-stream workload; ignore this marker.
Explain why database indexes speed up reads but slow down writes. Use a concrete library-catalog analogy, discuss selectivity and give one practical rule for choosing a compound index. Write about 220 words.
responses.text:
An index is like a library’s card catalog: instead of scanning every shelf (a table scan), you look up a subject heading and jump straight to the right shelf. Reads speed up because the catalog is sorted and narrow, so the database can binary-search it and fetch only matching rows.

Selectivity decides how helpful the catalog is. A high-selectivity key—like ISBN—points to one book, so the index is tiny and lookups are fast. A low-selectivity key—like “Fiction”—points to thousands of books; the index is large, and the database may decide a full scan is cheaper.

Writes slow down because every insert, update, or delete must also update the catalog: add a card, refile cards, and maintain the index’s structure (e.g., B-tree balancing). More indexes mean more bookkeeping per write, plus extra I/O and locking.

Practical rule for compound indexes: order columns by equality first,range second. For queries like WHERE author = 'Orwell' AND year > 1940, create (author, year). The equality column narrows the set; the range column then filters within it. Reversing the order wastes the range’s usefulness because the database can’t efficiently skip ahead.
